output.title: What churn signals hide before the customer leaves
output.body:
Most churn does not show up as a clean cancellation. It usually starts smaller: fewer orders, longer gaps between purchases, repeated support questions, or a customer quietly dropping one part of the service while the invoice keeps getting paid.

The useful distinction is between active signals and passive erosion. Active signals are the obvious ones: a cancellation notice, a failed payment, a sharp complaint. Those need a person to act now. Passive signals are the slower pattern changes that get missed until the customer is already halfway out the door.

For a small online shop, a simple illustration is this: if a customer used to buy every week and then goes three weeks with no order, that is not proof of churn. It is a signal worth reviewing.

The bounded workflow decision is not “can AI predict churn?” It is “can we flag these patterns from data we already have, then send them to manual review?” That might be a spreadsheet rule, a CRM filter, or a lightweight automation. Human approval stays in charge of the response.

Practical next step: pull order history, support tickets, login activity, and payment records for the last 12 months, then pick two or three customers who left or went quiet. Write down the first signal that was visible at the time. If you cannot find one, the problem may be the workflow, not the customer. A quiet customer is still a customer data point, unfortunately.
